subtype_info: Strongyloides colitis previously misdiagnosed as ulcerative colitis
title: Inflammatory bowel disease later diagnosed as strongyloides colitis in migrants to Canada: a case series
case_text:
A 64-year-old woman was referred to our unit for treatment of S. stercoralis infection, following identification of rhabditiform larvae on routine microscopic stool O&P examination. At consultation, the patient was clinically well. Aside from minimal abdominal discomfort, review of systems was unremarkable. She reported regular bowel movements without diarrhea or hematochezia. She denied skin or respiratory symptoms. Past medical history was notable for a diagnosis of UC 10 years prior to referral via colonic biopsies, with recommendation for follow-up colonoscopies every 3-5 years. Her only medication was 5-ASA, which she had been taking for a few years. Beyond the abnormal stool O&P, another notable laboratory finding was moderate peripheral eosinophilia of 1.18 x 109/L (reference < 0.4 x 109/L) from a CBC 6 months prior.
Given the patient's birth country of Nigeria and notable travel throughout the Caribbean over the prior decades, including to high-risk destinations for strongyloidiasis, such as Antigua, Barbados, Curacao, the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Haiti, and Puerto Rico, the timing of her exposure to Strongyloides spp. was unclear. Thus, a review of the previously obtained colonic tissue was requested to exclude signs of Strongyloides spp.-induced colitis. Routine blood work was performed and a pre-treatment Strongyloides spp. Serology was requested along with screening for HTLV-1/2. The patient was treated with two doses of ivermectin at 200 mug/kg 2 weeks apart.
Pre-treatment Strongyloides spp. serology was reactive with an optical density (OD) of 2.39 (non-reactive < 0.2), and eosinophilia persisted at 1.8 x 109/L. HTLV-1/2 testing was negative. Re-examination of colonic tissue demonstrated features consistent with Strongyloides colitis including distal attenuation of disease with sparing of the sigmoid colon and rectum, preservation of crypt architecture and goblet cell mucin, and eosinophilic infiltrates of the lamina propria. The patient's 5-ASA was held in light of the new findings. At 2 weeks post-treatment, the patient remained clinically well, with reduction in her eosinophil count to 0.4 x 109/L, and at 9 months after ivermectin treatment, she reported feeling very well, with complete resolution of her UC symptoms. Post-treatment, Strongyloides spp. serology revealed seroreduction to an OD of 0.65 (non-reactive < 0.2).

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Soil-Transmitted Helminths
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Strongyloides colitis previously misdiagnosed as ulcerative colitis
